theme: Why do you cast us off forever?
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 74. It is a communal lament over the destruction of the sanctuary. Notice how the psalmist reasons with God, recalling his past deeds and appealing to his covenant.
settingTheScene: Psalm 74 is a Maskil of Asaph. It was likely written after the destruction of the temple by the Babylonians, though the destruction of the northern sanctuaries by the Assyrians also fits. It is placed here as the Psalter’s response to the fall of the divided kingdoms. The congregation is bewildered, as Hosea predicted, and asks God how long and why.
observation: “O God, why do you cast us off forever? Why does your anger smoke against the sheep of your pasture?” (v. 1).
“Remember your congregation, which you have purchased of old, which you have redeemed to be the tribe of your heritage” (v. 2).
“Your foes have roared in the midst of your meeting place; they set up their own signs for signs” (v. 4).
“They said to themselves, We will utterly subdue them; they burned all the meeting places of God in the land” (v. 8).
“We do not see our signs; there is no longer any prophet, and there is none among us who knows how long” (v. 9).
“Yet God my King is from of old, working salvation in the midst of the earth” (v. 12).
“Yours is the day, yours also the night; you have established the heavenly lights and the sun” (v. 16).
“Have regard for the covenant… Arise, O God, defend your cause” (vv. 20, 22).
interpretation:
The psalm opens with the question, “Why?” It does not hold back. God has cast off his people, and his anger smokes. The picture of “the sheep of your pasture” reminds us that God is a shepherd. How can a shepherd be angry at his own sheep? The psalmist asks God to look at what has happened. He asks him to walk through the ruins.

The description of the destruction is vivid. The enemies hacked the carved work with axes and hatchets. They burned the sanctuary and profaned God’s dwelling place. The worst part is that God’s own place has been dishonored, and his name reviled. The psalmist is grieved less for his own loss than for the offense to God.

Verse 9 is a sorrowful statement: “We do not see our signs; there is no longer any prophet.” The people are in the silence Amos predicted, a famine of hearing the word of the LORD. No prophet knows how long. It is one of the hardest places for faith: when there is no word.

But in verse 12, a turn: “Yet God my King is from of old.” The word “yet” is the pivot. The psalmist recalls what God did: dividing the sea, breaking the heads of the sea monsters, drying up ever-flowing rivers. He remembers the creation: day and night, sun and moon, boundaries of the earth, summer and winter. The God who ordered the cosmos is the same God who is silent now. Memory becomes the foundation for hope.

The psalm ends with a series of petitions. “Have regard for the covenant.” “Arise, O God, defend your cause.” “Remember how the foolish scoff at you all the day.” The psalmist appeals to God’s own honor. He asks God to act for the sake of his own name and covenant. This is the pattern of prayer when everything seems lost: remember who God is, and ask him to act as he has promised.
connection: Jesus predicted the destruction of the temple (Matthew 24:2) and said, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). He is the true sanctuary that cannot be destroyed. Hebrews 8:1-2 speaks of the true tent. Mark 4:39 shows Jesus rebuking the storm, like God who “divided the sea.” Romans 8:35-39 assures us that nothing can separate us from God’s covenant love.
application:
When things fall apart, follow the psalmist’s pattern: state the complaint, then remember what God has done.

Pray for those whose places of worship have been destroyed or who cannot worship freely.

Pray, “Have regard for the covenant,” knowing that God has bound himself to you in Christ.
prayerPrompts: Tell God about what feels like abandonment.
Remember aloud that he is King from of old.
Ask him to remember his covenant and his people.
